notes.title: Key facts by topic
notes.html:
Physicist’s toolkit: vectors, units, estimation

  • Dimensions and units — Every term in a valid equation has the same dimensions. Checking units catches most algebra mistakes. Example: x = ½at² has dimensions L = (L/T²)T².
  • Estimation — Physicists estimate to the nearest power of ten (Fermi problems). Break the problem into numbers you know, multiply, and check the order of magnitude.
  • Vectors — A vector has magnitude and direction. Components: A_x = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ. Add components, not magnitudes. Dot product A·B = AB cos θ; cross product magnitude AB sin θ.

Motion & kinematics

  • Speed — Speed tells how far something goes in a certain time. Going 60 km in 2 hours is 30 kilometers every hour.
  • Velocity and direction — Velocity is speed with a direction. Walking 3 m/s north and 3 m/s south have the same speed but opposite velocities.
  • Acceleration — Acceleration is how fast velocity changes. A car going from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s gains 5 m/s every second.

Forces & Newton’s laws

  • Pushes and pulls — A force is a push or a pull. It is measured in newtons (N). One newton is about the weight of a small apple.
  • Balanced and unbalanced forces — If forces balance, the motion does not change: a book on a table stays put. An unbalanced (net) force changes the motion.
  • Newton's first law — An object keeps doing what it is doing, at rest or moving in a straight line at steady speed, unless a net force acts on it. This is inertia.

Work, energy & power

  • Energy and work — Energy is the ability to make things change. Work is energy transferred by a force: lifting a box takes work.
  • Kinetic energy — Moving things have kinetic energy. It grows with mass and with the square of speed: doubling the speed makes the energy four times bigger.
  • Potential energy — Raised things can fall, so they store gravitational potential energy.

Momentum & collisions

  • Momentum — Momentum is mass times velocity. A heavy truck and a fast bullet can both be hard to stop.
  • Impulse — A force acting for a time changes momentum. A longer time means a smaller force for the same change, which is why airbags help.
  • Conservation of momentum — In a collision with no outside force, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.

Rotation & torque

  • Angular motion — Rotation uses angle θ (radians), angular velocity ω = Δθ/Δt and angular acceleration α = Δω/Δt. The equations match straight-line motion: ω = ω₀ + αt and θ = ω₀t + ½αt².
  • Torque — A force turns an object only if it acts at a distance from the pivot. Torque = r F sin θ, where θ is the angle between the lever arm r and the force.
  • Moment of inertia — I measures how hard it is to change rotation. It grows with mass and with distance from the axis squared. Point masses: I = Σmr². Solid disk about its centre: ½MR². Hoop: MR². Rod about its centre: ML²/12.

Circular motion & gravity

  • Going around — Anything moving in a circle is always turning, so its velocity keeps changing direction. That means it is accelerating even at constant speed.
  • Speed on a circle — One lap is 2πr long. If it takes time T, speed v = 2πr/T.
  • Centripetal acceleration — The acceleration points to the center and equals v²/r. The net force pointing in is the centripetal force, F = mv²/r.

Gravitation & orbits

  • Newton's law of gravitation — Every pair of masses attracts with force F = GMm/r², with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². Field strength at distance r from mass M is g = GM/r².
  • Orbits — For a circular orbit gravity supplies the centripetal force: GM/r² = v²/r, so v = √(GM/r). Higher orbits are slower.
  • Kepler's third law — T² is proportional to r³. If you know one orbit you can find another: (T₂/T₁)² = (r₂/r₁)³.

Oscillations & SHM

  • Oscillation — An oscillation repeats. The period T is the time for one cycle. The frequency f = 1/T is cycles per second (hertz).
  • Restoring force — In simple harmonic motion the force always points back toward equilibrium and grows with displacement: F = −kx. This is Hooke's law.
  • Mass on a spring — The period depends on mass and stiffness only, not on the amplitude: bigger mass is slower, stiffer spring is faster.

Calculus-based mechanics (AP C)

  • Motion with calculus — Velocity is the derivative of position, and acceleration the derivative of velocity. Going backwards: v = ∫a dt and x = ∫v dt, with initial conditions as constants.
  • Work from a variable force — When force changes with position, work is the area under the F–x curve: W = ∫F dx.
  • Impulse from a variable force — Impulse is the area under the F–t curve: J = ∫F dt = Δp.

Fluids

  • Pressure — Pressure is force per area. Units: pascals (Pa), one newton per square metre.
  • Pressure in a fluid — Pressure grows with depth: the weight of the fluid above pushes down. Gauge pressure is ρgh. Atmospheric pressure adds about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.
  • Pascal's principle — Pressure added to a confined fluid spreads everywhere. A hydraulic lift trades distance for force: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

Waves & sound

  • Waves carry energy — A wave moves energy without moving matter along with it. A stadium wave moves around the arena while each person only stands up and sits down.
  • Frequency and period — Frequency f is how many waves pass each second (hertz). Period T is the time for one wave. f = 1/T.
  • Wavelength and speed — The wavelength λ is the length of one wave. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.

Electromagnetic waves & wave optics

  • Electromagnetic waves — Changing E and B fields sustain each other and travel at c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Radio, light and X-rays differ only in frequency: c = fλ.
  • Refraction — Light slows in matter: n = c/v. At a boundary n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Past the critical angle, sin θ_c = n₂/n₁, light is totally reflected.
  • Double-slit interference — Two slits make bright fringes where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths. Fringe spacing on a screen: Δy = λL/d.

Light & optics

  • Light travels in straight lines — Light moves in straight rays at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. We see an object when its light reaches our eyes. Shadows form where light is blocked.
  • Reflection — A ray hits a mirror and bounces off. The angle in equals the angle out, both measured from the normal (the line at 90° to the surface).
  • Refraction — Light bends when it passes between materials because it changes speed. The index of refraction is n = c/v. Snell's law links the angles.

Heat & thermodynamics

  • Heat and temperature — Temperature measures how fast the particles jiggle on average. Heat is energy that flows from hot to cold. Both are not the same thing.
  • Specific heat — Q = mcΔT gives the heat needed to change a temperature. Water has c = 4186 J/(kg·°C), which is why it warms slowly.
  • Phase changes — Melting or boiling takes energy with no temperature change. Q = mL, with L the latent heat. For water, L_fusion ≈ 334 kJ/kg and L_vaporization ≈ 2260 kJ/kg.

Gases & thermodynamics

  • Ideal gas — For a gas of n moles, PV = nRT with R = 8.31 J/(mol·K) and T in kelvin. Add 273 to a Celsius temperature.
  • Gas laws — At fixed amount, P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. At fixed T, pressure and volume are inversely related (Boyle).
  • Kinetic theory — Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules: for one molecule of a monatomic gas, KE = (3/2)k_BT. The internal energy of n moles is (3/2)nRT.

Electric fields & charge

  • Charge — Matter has positive and negative charge. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract. Charge is measured in coulombs (C). One electron has charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
  • Coulomb's law — The force between two point charges is F = kq₁q₂/r², with k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Doubling the distance cuts the force to a quarter.
  • Electric field — The field E at a point is the force per unit charge, E = F/q. A point charge makes E = kQ/r². Field lines point away from positive charge.

Electric potential & Gauss’s law

  • Electric potential — Potential is energy per charge, V = U/q, measured in volts. A point charge makes V = kq/r with k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
  • Work and potential difference — Moving a charge q through a potential difference ΔV changes its energy by qΔV. A charge released from rest gains kinetic energy qΔV.
  • Uniform fields — Between parallel plates E is uniform and V = Ed. The field points from high to low potential.

Ohm’s law & DC circuits

  • Charge, current and voltage — Current is how much charge flows past a point each second. Voltage is the push that makes charge flow, like water pressure in a pipe.
  • Resistance — Resistance is how much a part holds back current, like a narrow pipe. It is measured in ohms (Ω).
  • Ohm's law — Voltage, current and resistance are linked: V = I × R. Double the voltage and the current doubles.

Kirchhoff & network analysis

  • Nodes and loops — A node is where wires meet. A loop is any closed path. Kirchhoff's two laws apply to every circuit, however tangled.
  • Current law — The current into a node equals the current out. Charge does not pile up.
  • Voltage law — Going once around any loop, the voltage rises equal the voltage drops. The sum is zero.

Capacitors, inductors & transients

  • Capacitor basics — A capacitor stores energy in an electric field. Q = CV and the energy is ½CV². Units: farads (F), often µF or nF.
  • RC charging — Through a resistor a capacitor charges gradually. The time constant is τ = RC. After one τ it reaches 63% of the final voltage; after 5τ it is essentially full.
  • RC discharging — Discharging, the voltage falls as V = V₀e^(−t/τ). After one τ it is 37% of the start.

Magnetism & induction

  • Magnetic fields — Magnets and moving charges make magnetic fields, measured in tesla (T). Field lines run from north to south outside the magnet.
  • Force on a wire — A wire of length L carrying current I in a field B feels force F = BIL when the wire is at right angles to the field.
  • Force on a charge — A charge q moving at speed v across field B feels F = qvB. The force is sideways, so the charge goes in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB).

Magnetic forces, Ampère & Faraday (AP E&M)

  • Magnetic force on a charge — A charge moving across a magnetic field feels a force F = qvB sin θ, at right angles to both v and B (right-hand rule). The force does no work, so speed stays constant.
  • Circular paths — A charge moving at right angles to B goes in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB), with period T = 2πm/(qB).
  • Force on a wire — A current-carrying wire in a field feels F = BIL sin θ.

AC, phasors & impedance

  • What AC means — Alternating current swings back and forth like a sine wave. Wall power is 60 Hz in the US: 60 full cycles each second.
  • RMS values — The RMS value gives the same heating as DC. For a sine wave V_rms = V_peak/√2 ≈ 0.707 V_peak. US outlets are 120 V rms.
  • Reactance — A capacitor resists AC by X_C = 1/(2πfC); an inductor by X_L = 2πfL. Units: ohms. Capacitors pass high frequencies, inductors pass low ones.

Resonance & filters

  • Frequency response — A filter treats frequencies differently. A low-pass filter keeps low frequencies, a high-pass keeps high ones, and a band-pass keeps a range.
  • RC cutoff — An RC filter drops to 70.7% (−3 dB) of the input at the cutoff frequency f_c = 1/(2πRC).
  • Decibels — Decibels compare sizes on a log scale: dB = 20 log₁₀(V_out/V_in) for voltage. Every factor of 10 is 20 dB; halving is about −6 dB.

Diodes, transistors & op-amps

  • Diodes — A diode lets current go one way. Silicon needs about 0.7 V forward; an LED needs roughly 2 V. Always add a series resistor.
  • LED resistor — The resistor drops the leftover voltage: R = (V_supply − V_LED)/I.
  • Rectifiers — A diode on an AC source blocks the negative half (half-wave). A bridge of four diodes flips the negative half (full-wave). A capacitor then smooths it.

Digital logic

  • Binary — Computers use only 0 and 1. Each place is a power of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... so 1011₂ = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.
  • Hexadecimal — Hex uses 16 digits (0–9, A–F). One hex digit equals four bits: A = 1010, F = 1111.
  • Logic gates — AND is 1 only if both inputs are 1. OR is 1 if either is 1. NOT flips the bit. NAND and NOR are the opposites of AND and OR.

Power & transformers

  • Electric power — Power is P = VI = I²R = V²/R, in watts. A kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the energy of 1 kW used for 1 hour, or 3.6 million joules.
  • Why power lines use high voltage — Wire loss is I²R. Raising the voltage by 10× cuts the current for the same power by 10× and the loss by 100×.
  • Efficiency — Efficiency = useful output power ÷ input power. The difference leaves as heat.

Quantum & nuclear physics

  • Photons — Light comes in packets. A photon has energy E = hf = hc/λ. A handy form: E (eV) = 1240 / λ (nm).
  • Photoelectric effect — A photon frees an electron only if its energy exceeds the metal's work function φ. The fastest electrons leave with KE_max = hf − φ. Brighter light means more electrons, not faster ones.
  • Matter waves — Particles have a wavelength λ = h/p. Electrons diffract, which is why electron microscopes see fine detail.

written: Why do heavy and light objects fall together?
Gravity pulls harder on a heavier object, but a heavier object also resists acceleration more. The two effects cancel, so all objects fall with the same acceleration when air drag is ignored.
Why does a series circuit go dark when one bulb is removed?
There is only one path. Removing a part breaks the loop, so the current stops everywhere.
bench: Ohm's law with a battery and bulb
Measure the voltage across and current through one, two and three bulbs in series. Plot V against I and find the slope.
Time ten swings of strings with different lengths. Compare period against length.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. What force pairs with the book's weight in Newton's third law: the table's push up on the book, or the book's pull on Earth?
text: gravitational pull of the book on earth
sol: Third-law pairs act on different objects.
Earth pulls the book down, so the book pulls Earth up. The table's push is a different interaction.
questions.w: Earth pulls the book down, so the book pulls Earth up. The table's push is a different interaction.

questions.q: A solid sphere, a solid disk and a hoop (same mass and radius) are released together from rest at the top of a ramp and roll without slipping. Which reaches the bottom first?
sol: A smaller moment of inertia per mass means less of the energy goes into spinning, so more goes into moving down the slope.
I/(mR²): sphere 2/5, disk 1/2, hoop 1. The sphere wins, the hoop loses.

A charged particle moves through a magnetic field. The magnetic force on it…
o: Does no work, so its speed stays constant
Speeds it up when it points along the motion
Acts along the direction of the field
sol: F = qv × B is always perpendicular to v.
A force perpendicular to the motion does no work.
The speed is unchanged; only the direction changes.
questions.w: The speed is unchanged; only the direction changes.

o: The units of √(g/L) are 1/s, not seconds
The formula has a factor of 2π
It does not include the mass
sol: So √(g/L) has units 1/s, not s. Dimensional analysis rejects it. (Also: longer pendulums should be slower.)

questions.q: Which is the best estimate for the number of seconds in one year?
sol: The right order of magnitude is 10⁷.
questions.w: The right order of magnitude is 10⁷.

kin: Speed tells how far something goes in a certain time. Going 60 km in 2 hours is 30 kilometers every hour.
Velocity is speed with a direction. Walking 3 m/s north and 3 m/s south have the same speed but opposite velocities.
Acceleration is how fast velocity changes. A car going from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s gains 5 m/s every second.
Near Earth, anything in free fall (no air drag) speeds up by about 9.8 m/s every second, no matter its mass.
When acceleration is steady: v = v₀ + at, and d = v₀t + ½at². Pick the one that has the quantities you know.
v = v₀ + at;  d = v₀t + ½at²
On a position-time graph, slope is velocity. On a velocity-time graph, slope is acceleration and area is displacement.
ohm: Current is how much charge flows past a point each second. Voltage is the push that makes charge flow, like water pressure in a pipe.
Resistance is how much a part holds back current, like a narrow pipe. It is measured in ohms (Ω).
Voltage, current and resistance are linked: V = I × R. Double the voltage and the current doubles.
In series there is one path. The same current goes through every part, resistances add, and voltages share the supply.
In parallel there are branches. Every branch gets the full supply voltage, and the currents add.
Power is how fast energy is used. A 60 W bulb uses 60 joules every second.
frc: A force is a push or a pull. It is measured in newtons (N). One newton is about the weight of a small apple.
If forces balance, the motion does not change: a book on a table stays put. An unbalanced (net) force changes the motion.
An object keeps doing what it is doing, at rest or moving in a straight line at steady speed, unless a net force acts on it. This is inertia.
The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration. Push twice as hard and it accelerates twice as fast. Double the mass and it accelerates half as much.
Mass is how much matter you have (kg). Weight is the pull of gravity on it (N). Weight = mass × g, with g ≈ 10 N/kg near Earth.
Friction opposes sliding. Its maximum size is f = μN, where N is the push of the surface on the object and μ depends on the two surfaces.
When object A pushes on B, B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force. The two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel.
On a slope, gravity splits into a part along the slope, mg sin θ, and a part into the slope, mg cos θ.
nrg: Energy is the ability to make things change. Work is energy transferred by a force: lifting a box takes work.
Moving things have kinetic energy. It grows with mass and with the square of speed: doubling the speed makes the energy four times bigger.
Raised things can fall, so they store gravitational potential energy.
Energy is never created or destroyed. It changes form. Without friction, KE + PE stays the same along a path.
Power is how fast energy is used or work is done. One watt is one joule per second.
A stretched spring pulls back with F = kx and stores energy ½kx².
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ energy in. No machine is 100% efficient because some energy always turns into heat.
mom: Momentum is mass times velocity. A heavy truck and a fast bullet can both be hard to stop.
A force acting for a time changes momentum. A longer time means a smaller force for the same change, which is why airbags help.
In a collision with no outside force, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.
If objects stick, they move off together: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v. Kinetic energy is lost to heat and deformation.
In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are kept. Equal masses swap velocities.
If two objects start at rest and push apart, their momenta are equal and opposite. The lighter one moves faster.
A rocket pushes gas backward and gains forward momentum. It works in space because it does not push against anything outside.
On a force-time graph, the area under the curve is the impulse.
cir: Anything moving in a circle is always turning, so its velocity keeps changing direction. That means it is accelerating even at constant speed.
One lap is 2πr long. If it takes time T, speed v = 2πr/T.
The acceleration points to the center and equals v²/r. The net force pointing in is the centripetal force, F = mv²/r.
Centripetal force is not a new force. It is tension, gravity, friction or a normal force pointing toward the center.
Every pair of masses attracts. F = Gm₁m₂/r². Double the distance and the force becomes one quarter.
A satellite is falling around Earth. Gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r).
g = GM/r². Moving from the surface to twice the Earth's radius from the center makes g four times smaller.
At the top of a vertical loop, gravity and the normal force both point down. The slowest speed that keeps contact is v = √(gr).
wav: A wave moves energy without moving matter along with it. A stadium wave moves around the arena while each person only stands up and sits down.
Frequency f is how many waves pass each second (hertz). Period T is the time for one wave. f = 1/T.
The wavelength λ is the length of one wave. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.
In a transverse wave the particles move sideways to the motion (light, a rope). In a longitudinal wave they move back and forth along it (sound).
Sound is a longitudinal wave in air. It travels about 340 m/s in air, faster in water and fastest in solids.
Waves add. Crest meets crest: bigger wave. Crest meets trough: they cancel. Two close frequencies make beats at |f₁ − f₂|.
On a string fixed at both ends, only certain waves fit: fₙ = n·v/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3, … This is how guitars and organs choose notes.
Intensity falls with the square of distance. Every 10 dB is ten times the intensity. A 10 dB increase sounds about twice as loud.
opt: Light moves in straight rays at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. We see an object when its light reaches our eyes. Shadows form where light is blocked.
A ray hits a mirror and bounces off. The angle in equals the angle out, both measured from the normal (the line at 90° to the surface).
Light bends when it passes between materials because it changes speed. The index of refraction is n = c/v. Snell's law links the angles.
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
Going from a slow material to a faster one, the ray bends away from the normal. Past the critical angle sin θc = n₂/n₁ all the light reflects. Optical fibres use this.
A converging lens or concave mirror bends rays to a focus at distance f. The thin-lens equation connects object distance d₀, image distance dᵢ and focal length f.
thm: Temperature measures how fast the particles jiggle on average. Heat is energy that flows from hot to cold. Both are not the same thing.
Q = mcΔT gives the heat needed to change a temperature. Water has c = 4186 J/(kg·°C), which is why it warms slowly.
Melting or boiling takes energy with no temperature change. Q = mL, with L the latent heat. For water, L_fusion ≈ 334 kJ/kg and L_vaporization ≈ 2260 kJ/kg.
For a fixed amount of gas, PV/T stays constant, with T in kelvin. K = °C + 273. The ideal gas law is PV = nRT.
An engine takes heat Qh from a hot source, does work W and dumps Qc. Efficiency is e = W/Qh = 1 − Qc/Qh. The best possible efficiency is 1 − Tc/Th (kelvin).
est: Matter has positive and negative charge. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract. Charge is measured in coulombs (C). One electron has charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
The force between two point charges is F = kq₁q₂/r², with k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Doubling the distance cuts the force to a quarter.
The field E at a point is the force per unit charge, E = F/q. A point charge makes E = kQ/r². Field lines point away from positive charge.
Potential V is energy per unit charge, in volts. A charge q moved through a potential difference V gains energy qV. A uniform field has V = Ed.
Two plates storing charge: Q = CV. The energy stored is ½CV². Parallel-plate: C = ε₀A/d.
kvl: A node is where wires meet. A loop is any closed path. Kirchhoff's two laws apply to every circuit, however tangled.
The current into a node equals the current out. Charge does not pile up.
Going once around any loop, the voltage rises equal the voltage drops. The sum is zero.
Series resistors share voltage in proportion to resistance: V₁ = V·R₁/(R₁ + R₂). Parallel resistors share current: I₁ = I·R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
Any two-terminal linear network acts like a voltage source V_th in series with R_th. A load takes maximum power when R_L = R_th.
rc: A capacitor stores energy in an electric field. Q = CV and the energy is ½CV². Units: farads (F), often µF or nF.
Through a resistor a capacitor charges gradually. The time constant is τ = RC. After one τ it reaches 63% of the final voltage; after 5τ it is essentially full.
Discharging, the voltage falls as V = V₀e^(−t/τ). After one τ it is 37% of the start.
A coil resists changes in current. V = L·ΔI/Δt and the stored energy is ½LI². In an RL circuit τ = L/R.
Capacitors in parallel add: C = C₁ + C₂. In series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. Inductors behave like resistors.
ac: Alternating current swings back and forth like a sine wave. Wall power is 60 Hz in the US: 60 full cycles each second.
The RMS value gives the same heating as DC. For a sine wave V_rms = V_peak/√2 ≈ 0.707 V_peak. US outlets are 120 V rms.
A capacitor resists AC by X_C = 1/(2πfC); an inductor by X_L = 2πfL. Units: ohms. Capacitors pass high frequencies, inductors pass low ones.
Resistance and reactance combine at right angles: |Z| = √(R² + X²) for a series RL or RC circuit. Ohm's law becomes V = IZ.
Only the resistive part uses real power: P = V·I·cos φ, where cos φ = R/|Z| is the power factor.
flt: A filter treats frequencies differently. A low-pass filter keeps low frequencies, a high-pass keeps high ones, and a band-pass keeps a range.
An RC filter drops to 70.7% (−3 dB) of the input at the cutoff frequency f_c = 1/(2πRC).
Decibels compare sizes on a log scale: dB = 20 log₁₀(V_out/V_in) for voltage. Every factor of 10 is 20 dB; halving is about −6 dB.
A series LC circuit has the lowest impedance at f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)), where X_L = X_C. Radios tune by changing this frequency.
Q = f₀/bandwidth tells how sharp the resonance is. A series RLC has Q = X_L/R at resonance.
dev: A diode lets current go one way. Silicon needs about 0.7 V forward; an LED needs roughly 2 V. Always add a series resistor.
The resistor drops the leftover voltage: R = (V_supply − V_LED)/I.
A diode on an AC source blocks the negative half (half-wave). A bridge of four diodes flips the negative half (full-wave). A capacitor then smooths it.
A small base current controls a big collector current: I_C = β·I_B. It works as a switch or an amplifier.
An op-amp with negative feedback has two golden rules: no current into the inputs and equal input voltages. Inverting gain = −R_f/R_in; non-inverting gain = 1 + R_f/R_in.
dig: Computers use only 0 and 1. Each place is a power of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... so 1011₂ = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.
Hex uses 16 digits (0–9, A–F). One hex digit equals four bits: A = 1010, F = 1111.
AND is 1 only if both inputs are 1. OR is 1 if either is 1. NOT flips the bit. NAND and NOR are the opposites of AND and OR.
A truth table lists the output for every input combination. n inputs give 2ⁿ rows.
An n-bit converter splits its range into 2ⁿ levels. Step size = full-scale voltage ÷ 2ⁿ.
mag: Magnets and moving charges make magnetic fields, measured in tesla (T). Field lines run from north to south outside the magnet.
A wire of length L carrying current I in a field B feels force F = BIL when the wire is at right angles to the field.
A charge q moving at speed v across field B feels F = qvB. The force is sideways, so the charge goes in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB).
A changing magnetic flux induces a voltage: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt (Faraday's law). Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change.
Two coils on one iron core: V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁. A step-up transformer raises voltage and lowers current.
pwr: Power is P = VI = I²R = V²/R, in watts. A kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the energy of 1 kW used for 1 hour, or 3.6 million joules.
Why power lines use high voltage
Wire loss is I²R. Raising the voltage by 10× cuts the current for the same power by 10× and the loss by 100×.
Efficiency = useful output power ÷ input power. The difference leaves as heat.
Power plants use three sine waves 120° apart. Total power is √3·V_line·I_line·cos φ.
rot: Rotation uses angle θ (radians), angular velocity ω = Δθ/Δt and angular acceleration α = Δω/Δt. The equations match straight-line motion: ω = ω₀ + αt and θ = ω₀t + ½αt².
A force turns an object only if it acts at a distance from the pivot. Torque = r F sin θ, where θ is the angle between the lever arm r and the force.

I measures how hard it is to change rotation. It grows with mass and with distance from the axis squared. Point masses: I = Σmr². Solid disk about its centre: ½MR². Hoop: MR². Rod about its centre: ML²/12.
Net torque = I α. A bigger moment of inertia means a smaller angular acceleration for the same torque.
A spinning object stores energy ½Iω². A rolling object has both ½mv² and ½Iω².
L = Iω. With no net external torque L is conserved: a skater who pulls her arms in lowers I, so ω rises.
The contact point is at rest, so v = ωR. Rolling down a slope the energy splits between moving and spinning, so rolling objects accelerate more slowly than sliding ones.
sho: An oscillation repeats. The period T is the time for one cycle. The frequency f = 1/T is cycles per second (hertz).
In simple harmonic motion the force always points back toward equilibrium and grows with displacement: F = −kx. This is Hooke's law.
The period depends on mass and stiffness only, not on the amplitude: bigger mass is slower, stiffer spring is faster.
For small angles a pendulum has period T = 2π√(L/g). It does not depend on the mass.
Energy swaps between kinetic and potential. Total energy ½kA² is constant. Speed is greatest at equilibrium: v_max = Aω with ω = √(k/m).
Position is a cosine (or sine) of time. Velocity leads position by a quarter cycle. Acceleration is −ω² x.
flu: Pressure is force per area. Units: pascals (Pa), one newton per square metre.
Pressure grows with depth: the weight of the fluid above pushes down. Gauge pressure is ρgh. Atmospheric pressure adds about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.
Pressure added to a confined fluid spreads everywhere. A hydraulic lift trades distance for force: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
A fluid pushes up with a force equal to the weight of the fluid the object pushes aside (Archimedes). F_B = ρ_fluid V_displaced g.
An incompressible fluid does not pile up: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Fluid speeds up in a narrow pipe.
Along a streamline, P + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant. Fast fluid means low pressure. Draining from a hole at depth h leaves at v = √(2gh).
gas: For a gas of n moles, PV = nRT with R = 8.31 J/(mol·K) and T in kelvin. Add 273 to a Celsius temperature.
At fixed amount, P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. At fixed T, pressure and volume are inversely related (Boyle).
Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules: for one molecule of a monatomic gas, KE = (3/2)k_BT. The internal energy of n moles is (3/2)nRT.
A gas doing work expands. At constant pressure W = PΔV. On a P–V graph, work is the area under the curve.
The internal energy changes by the heat added minus the work done by the gas.
An engine takes Q_h from a hot reservoir, does work W, and dumps Q_c. Efficiency e = W/Q_h. No engine beats the Carnot limit 1 − T_c/T_h (kelvin).
Heat flows by itself from hot to cold, and the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
mod: Light comes in packets. A photon has energy E = hf = hc/λ. A handy form: E (eV) = 1240 / λ (nm).
A photon frees an electron only if its energy exceeds the metal's work function φ. The fastest electrons leave with KE_max = hf − φ. Brighter light means more electrons, not faster ones.
Particles have a wavelength λ = h/p. Electrons diffract, which is why electron microscopes see fine detail.
Hydrogen energy levels are E_n = −13.6 eV / n². A photon is emitted or absorbed when the electron jumps between levels.
Unstable nuclei decay at random, but a large sample halves every half-life: N = N₀ (½)^(t/T½).
Mass is a form of energy: E = mc². In nuclear reactions the lost mass shows up as energy: 1 u of mass equals 931.5 MeV.
gau: Potential is energy per charge, V = U/q, measured in volts. A point charge makes V = kq/r with k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
Moving a charge q through a potential difference ΔV changes its energy by qΔV. A charge released from rest gains kinetic energy qΔV.
Between parallel plates E is uniform and V = Ed. The field points from high to low potential.
The electric flux through a closed surface depends only on the charge inside: Φ = Q_enc/ε₀ with ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²). Symmetry then gives E.
Point charge: E = kq/r². Long line of charge λ: E = λ/(2πε₀r). Infinite sheet σ: E = σ/(2ε₀). Inside a conductor in equilibrium E = 0.
Two plates store charge: Q = CV. A parallel-plate capacitor has C = ε₀A/d, and stores energy ½CV². A dielectric multiplies C by κ.
lor: A charge moving across a magnetic field feels a force F = qvB sin θ, at right angles to both v and B (right-hand rule). The force does no work, so speed stays constant.
A charge moving at right angles to B goes in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB), with period T = 2πm/(qB).
A current-carrying wire in a field feels F = BIL sin θ.
A long straight wire makes B = μ₀I/(2πr), with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. A solenoid has B = μ₀nI inside, where n is turns per metre.
A changing magnetic flux induces an emf: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt. Flux Φ = BA cos θ.
The induced current opposes the change that caused it. A rod of length L moving at v across a field B has emf ε = BLv.
mxw: Changing E and B fields sustain each other and travel at c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Radio, light and X-rays differ only in frequency: c = fλ.
Light slows in matter: n = c/v. At a boundary n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Past the critical angle, sin θ_c = n₂/n₁, light is totally reflected.
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
Two slits make bright fringes where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths. Fringe spacing on a screen: Δy = λL/d.
A slit of width a gives dark fringes where a sin θ = mλ. A narrower slit spreads the light more.
Polarizers pass one direction of the electric field. Unpolarized light loses half its intensity. Polarized light follows Malus's law I = I₀ cos²θ.
Reflections from the top and bottom of a thin film interfere. A reflection off a slower medium flips the wave (half a cycle). Film thickness then sets which colours cancel.
cal: Velocity is the derivative of position, and acceleration the derivative of velocity. Going backwards: v = ∫a dt and x = ∫v dt, with initial conditions as constants.
When force changes with position, work is the area under the F–x curve: W = ∫F dx.
Impulse is the area under the F–t curve: J = ∫F dt = Δp.
Force is minus the slope of the potential energy curve: F = −dU/dx. Equilibrium is where the slope is zero; stable where U has a minimum.
For continuous mass: x_cm = ∫x dm / ∫dm. For a rod with density λ(x), dm = λ dx.
I = ∫r² dm. Uniform rod about its end: ML²/3. About its centre: ML²/12.
orb: Every pair of masses attracts with force F = GMm/r², with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². Field strength at distance r from mass M is g = GM/r².
For a circular orbit gravity supplies the centripetal force: GM/r² = v²/r, so v = √(GM/r). Higher orbits are slower.
T² is proportional to r³. If you know one orbit you can find another: (T₂/T₁)² = (r₂/r₁)³.
With zero at infinity U = −GMm/r. It is negative: you must add energy to escape.
Total energy of a circular orbit is E = −GMm/(2r). KE = −E and U = 2E.
Escape means total energy zero: ½mv² = GMm/r, so v_esc = √(2GM/r), which is √2 times the circular-orbit speed.
dim: Every term in a valid equation has the same dimensions. Checking units catches most algebra mistakes. Example: x = ½at² has dimensions L = (L/T²)T².
Physicists estimate to the nearest power of ten (Fermi problems). Break the problem into numbers you know, multiply, and check the order of magnitude.
A vector has magnitude and direction. Components: A_x = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ. Add components, not magnitudes. Dot product A·B = AB cos θ; cross product magnitude AB sin θ.
Every measurement has an uncertainty. For products and quotients relative uncertainties add (roughly). For sums, absolute uncertainties add.
Report no more digits than the least precise input supports. Keep extra digits in the middle of a calculation and round at the end.
Test a formula at extremes: if m → 0 or r → ∞ should the answer vanish, blow up or approach a known result? This is the fastest way to check an unfamiliar formula.

Charge flowing per second; measured in amperes.

cards.t: A force acting for a time changes momentum. A longer time means a smaller force for the same change, which is why airbags help.

lab.hook: Impulse = force × time = change in momentum.
lab.note: {=f*t|1} N·s. A longer stopping time needs less force for the same impulse (airbags!).

cards.t: In a collision with no outside force, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.

lab.hook: Two carts crash and stick. Total momentum before = after.

cards.t: If objects stick, they move off together: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v. Kinetic energy is lost to heat and deformation.
In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are kept. Equal masses swap velocities.
If two objects start at rest and push apart, their momenta are equal and opposite. The lighter one moves faster.
A rocket pushes gas backward and gains forward momentum. It works in space because it does not push against anything outside.
On a force-time graph, the area under the curve is the impulse.
Rotation uses angle θ (radians), angular velocity ω = Δθ/Δt and angular acceleration α = Δω/Δt. The equations match straight-line motion: ω = ω₀ + αt and θ = ω₀t + ½αt².
A force turns an object only if it acts at a distance from the pivot. Torque = r F sin θ, where θ is the angle between the lever arm r and the force.

I measures how hard it is to change rotation. It grows with mass and with distance from the axis squared. Point masses: I = Σmr². Solid disk about its centre: ½MR². Hoop: MR². Rod about its centre: ML²/12.

lessons.title: Newton's second law for rotation · Rotational kinetic energy

cards.t: Net torque = I α. A bigger moment of inertia means a smaller angular acceleration for the same torque.
A spinning object stores energy ½Iω². A rolling object has both ½mv² and ½Iω².
L = Iω. With no net external torque L is conserved: a skater who pulls her arms in lowers I, so ω rises.
The contact point is at rest, so v = ωR. Rolling down a slope the energy splits between moving and spinning, so rolling objects accelerate more slowly than sliding ones.

lessons.title: Going around · Speed on a circle

cards.t: Anything moving in a circle is always turning, so its velocity keeps changing direction. That means it is accelerating even at constant speed.
One lap is 2πr long. If it takes time T, speed v = 2πr/T.
The acceleration points to the center and equals v²/r. The net force pointing in is the centripetal force, F = mv²/r.

lab.hook: Going around a circle needs an inward pull.
lab.note: {=v^2/r|1} m/s². A tighter turn (small r) or a faster speed needs more.

lessons.title: What provides the force? · Gravity between masses

cards.t: Centripetal force is not a new force. It is tension, gravity, friction or a normal force pointing toward the center.
Every pair of masses attracts. F = Gm₁m₂/r². Double the distance and the force becomes one quarter.

lab.hook: Gravity gets weaker with distance squared.
lab.note: At {d} Earth radii from the center, gravity is {=1/d^2|3} times its surface value.

cards.t: A satellite is falling around Earth. Gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r).

lessons.title: Gravity changes with height · Loops and tops of circles

cards.t: g = GM/r². Moving from the surface to twice the Earth's radius from the center makes g four times smaller.
At the top of a vertical loop, gravity and the normal force both point down. The slowest speed that keeps contact is v = √(gr).
Every pair of masses attracts with force F = GMm/r², with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². Field strength at distance r from mass M is g = GM/r².
For a circular orbit gravity supplies the centripetal force: GM/r² = v²/r, so v = √(GM/r). Higher orbits are slower.
T² is proportional to r³. If you know one orbit you can find another: (T₂/T₁)² = (r₂/r₁)³.
With zero at infinity U = −GMm/r. It is negative: you must add energy to escape.
Total energy of a circular orbit is E = −GMm/(2r). KE = −E and U = 2E.
Escape means total energy zero: ½mv² = GMm/r, so v_esc = √(2GM/r), which is √2 times the circular-orbit speed.
An oscillation repeats. The period T is the time for one cycle. The frequency f = 1/T is cycles per second (hertz).
In simple harmonic motion the force always points back toward equilibrium and grows with displacement: F = −kx. This is Hooke's law.
The period depends on mass and stiffness only, not on the amplitude: bigger mass is slower, stiffer spring is faster.
For small angles a pendulum has period T = 2π√(L/g). It does not depend on the mass.
Energy swaps between kinetic and potential. Total energy ½kA² is constant. Speed is greatest at equilibrium: v_max = Aω with ω = √(k/m).
Position is a cosine (or sine) of time. Velocity leads position by a quarter cycle. Acceleration is −ω² x.

lessons.title: Motion with calculus · Work from a variable force

cards.t: Velocity is the derivative of position, and acceleration the derivative of velocity. Going backwards: v = ∫a dt and x = ∫v dt, with initial conditions as constants.
When force changes with position, work is the area under the F–x curve: W = ∫F dx.
Impulse is the area under the F–t curve: J = ∫F dt = Δp.

lessons.title: Force from potential energy · Centre of mass

cards.t: Force is minus the slope of the potential energy curve: F = −dU/dx. Equilibrium is where the slope is zero; stable where U has a minimum.
For continuous mass: x_cm = ∫x dm / ∫dm. For a rod with density λ(x), dm = λ dx.
I = ∫r² dm. Uniform rod about its end: ML²/3. About its centre: ML²/12.
Pressure is force per area. Units: pascals (Pa), one newton per square metre.
Pressure grows with depth: the weight of the fluid above pushes down. Gauge pressure is ρgh. Atmospheric pressure adds about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.
Pressure added to a confined fluid spreads everywhere. A hydraulic lift trades distance for force: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
A fluid pushes up with a force equal to the weight of the fluid the object pushes aside (Archimedes). F_B = ρ_fluid V_displaced g.
An incompressible fluid does not pile up: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Fluid speeds up in a narrow pipe.
Along a streamline, P + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant. Fast fluid means low pressure. Draining from a hole at depth h leaves at v = √(2gh).

lessons.title: Waves carry energy · Frequency and period

cards.t: A wave moves energy without moving matter along with it. A stadium wave moves around the arena while each person only stands up and sits down.
Frequency f is how many waves pass each second (hertz). Period T is the time for one wave. f = 1/T.

lab.hook: A wave: how many peaks pass each second?

cards.t: The wavelength λ is the length of one wave. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.

lab.hook: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.

cards.t: In a transverse wave the particles move sideways to the motion (light, a rope). In a longitudinal wave they move back and forth along it (sound).
Sound is a longitudinal wave in air. It travels about 340 m/s in air, faster in water and fastest in solids.

lab.hook: Sound travels about 343 m/s in air. How far is the lightning?

cards.t: Waves add. Crest meets crest: bigger wave. Crest meets trough: they cancel. Two close frequencies make beats at |f₁ − f₂|.
On a string fixed at both ends, only certain waves fit: fₙ = n·v/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3, … This is how guitars and organs choose notes.
Intensity falls with the square of distance. Every 10 dB is ten times the intensity. A 10 dB increase sounds about twice as loud.
Changing E and B fields sustain each other and travel at c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Radio, light and X-rays differ only in frequency: c = fλ.
Light slows in matter: n = c/v. At a boundary n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Past the critical angle, sin θ_c = n₂/n₁, light is totally reflected.
cards.f: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂

cards.t: Two slits make bright fringes where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths. Fringe spacing on a screen: Δy = λL/d.
A slit of width a gives dark fringes where a sin θ = mλ. A narrower slit spreads the light more.
Polarizers pass one direction of the electric field. Unpolarized light loses half its intensity. Polarized light follows Malus's law I = I₀ cos²θ.
Reflections from the top and bottom of a thin film interfere. A reflection off a slower medium flips the wave (half a cycle). Film thickness then sets which colours cancel.

lessons.title: Light travels in straight lines · Reflection

cards.t: Light moves in straight rays at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. We see an object when its light reaches our eyes. Shadows form where light is blocked.
A ray hits a mirror and bounces off. The angle in equals the angle out, both measured from the normal (the line at 90° to the surface).

lab.hook: Angle in = angle out.
lab.out: The ray hits at {a}° and leaves at {a}°.

cards.t: Light bends when it passes between materials because it changes speed. The index of refraction is n = c/v. Snell's law links the angles.
cards.f: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂

lab.hook: Light bends going into glass. Snell: sin θ₁ = n sin θ₂.
lab.note: Air → n = {n}: {a}° bends to {=asind(sind(a)/n)|1}°, toward the normal.

lessons.title: Total internal reflection · Lenses and mirrors

cards.t: Going from a slow material to a faster one, the ray bends away from the normal. Past the critical angle sin θc = n₂/n₁ all the light reflects. Optical fibres use this.
A converging lens or concave mirror bends rays to a focus at distance f. The thin-lens equation connects object distance d₀, image distance dᵢ and focal length f.

lab.hook: Move the object. Where does the image form?

cards.t: Temperature measures how fast the particles jiggle on average. Heat is energy that flows from hot to cold. Both are not the same thing.
Q = mcΔT gives the heat needed to change a temperature. Water has c = 4186 J/(kg·°C), which is why it warms slowly.

lab.hook: Heat needed to warm water.

cards.t: Melting or boiling takes energy with no temperature change. Q = mL, with L the latent heat. For water, L_fusion ≈ 334 kJ/kg and L_vaporization ≈ 2260 kJ/kg.
For a fixed amount of gas, PV/T stays constant, with T in kelvin. K = °C + 273. The ideal gas law is PV = nRT.

lab.hook: Squeeze a gas and its pressure rises.

cards.t: An engine takes heat Qh from a hot source, does work W and dumps Qc. Efficiency is e = W/Qh = 1 − Qc/Qh. The best possible efficiency is 1 − Tc/Th (kelvin).
For a gas of n moles, PV = nRT with R = 8.31 J/(mol·K) and T in kelvin. Add 273 to a Celsius temperature.
At fixed amount, P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. At fixed T, pressure and volume are inversely related (Boyle).
Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules: for one molecule of a monatomic gas, KE = (3/2)k_BT. The internal energy of n moles is (3/2)nRT.

lessons.title: Work by a gas · First law

cards.t: A gas doing work expands. At constant pressure W = PΔV. On a P–V graph, work is the area under the curve.
The internal energy changes by the heat added minus the work done by the gas.
An engine takes Q_h from a hot reservoir, does work W, and dumps Q_c. Efficiency e = W/Q_h. No engine beats the Carnot limit 1 − T_c/T_h (kelvin).
Heat flows by itself from hot to cold, and the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
Matter has positive and negative charge. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract. Charge is measured in coulombs (C). One electron has charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
The force between two point charges is F = kq₁q₂/r², with k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Doubling the distance cuts the force to a quarter.

lab.hook: Charges push or pull; double the distance makes the force 4 times weaker.

pre.q: Triple the distance between two charges. The force becomes…

cards.t: The field E at a point is the force per unit charge, E = F/q. A point charge makes E = kQ/r². Field lines point away from positive charge.
Potential V is energy per unit charge, in volts. A charge q moved through a potential difference V gains energy qV. A uniform field has V = Ed.
Two plates storing charge: Q = CV. The energy stored is ½CV². Parallel-plate: C = ε₀A/d.

lessons.title: Electric potential · Work and potential difference

cards.t: Potential is energy per charge, V = U/q, measured in volts. A point charge makes V = kq/r with k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
Moving a charge q through a potential difference ΔV changes its energy by qΔV. A charge released from rest gains kinetic energy qΔV.
Between parallel plates E is uniform and V = Ed. The field points from high to low potential.

lessons.title: Gauss's law · Field of simple shapes

cards.t: The electric flux through a closed surface depends only on the charge inside: Φ = Q_enc/ε₀ with ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²). Symmetry then gives E.
Point charge: E = kq/r². Long line of charge λ: E = λ/(2πε₀r). Infinite sheet σ: E = σ/(2ε₀). Inside a conductor in equilibrium E = 0.
Two plates store charge: Q = CV. A parallel-plate capacitor has C = ε₀A/d, and stores energy ½CV². A dielectric multiplies C by κ.
Current is how much charge flows past a point each second. Voltage is the push that makes charge flow, like water pressure in a pipe.

lab.hook: Voltage pushes. Current flows.
lab.note: A {v} V battery pushes {=v/r|2} A through {r} Ω.

cards.t: Resistance is how much a part holds back current, like a narrow pipe. It is measured in ohms (Ω).

lab.hook: Resistance is how hard the path is for current.
lab.note: Bigger resistance, less current: 10 V ÷ {r} Ω = {=10/r|2} A.

pre.q: If you double the resistance and keep the same battery, the current…
pre.why: I = V ÷ R. A bigger R makes a smaller I.

cards.t: Voltage, current and resistance are linked: V = I × R. Double the voltage and the current doubles.

lab.hook: Change V and R. Watch I change.
lab.take: I = V ÷ R. More voltage means more current; more resistance means less.

cards.t: In series there is one path. The same current goes through every part, resistances add, and voltages share the supply.
In parallel there are branches. Every branch gets the full supply voltage, and the currents add.
Power is how fast energy is used. A 60 W bulb uses 60 joules every second.

lab.hook: Power is energy per second: P = V × I.

cards.t: A node is where wires meet. A loop is any closed path. Kirchhoff's two laws apply to every circuit, however tangled.
The current into a node equals the current out. Charge does not pile up.
Going once around any loop, the voltage rises equal the voltage drops. The sum is zero.

lessons.title: Voltage and current dividers · Thevenin and maximum power

cards.t: Series resistors share voltage in proportion to resistance: V₁ = V·R₁/(R₁ + R₂). Parallel resistors share current: I₁ = I·R₂/(R₁ + R₂).

lab.hook: A voltage divider shares a battery between two resistors.

cards.t: Any two-terminal linear network acts like a voltage source V_th in series with R_th. A load takes maximum power when R_L = R_th.
A capacitor stores energy in an electric field. Q = CV and the energy is ½CV². Units: farads (F), often µF or nF.
Through a resistor a capacitor charges gradually. The time constant is τ = RC. After one τ it reaches 63% of the final voltage; after 5τ it is essentially full.

lab.hook: A capacitor charges quickly at first, then slows.
lab.out: After one τ ({t} s) it reaches 63% of 5 V = 3.16 V.

cards.t: Discharging, the voltage falls as V = V₀e^(−t/τ). After one τ it is 37% of the start.
A coil resists changes in current. V = L·ΔI/Δt and the stored energy is ½LI². In an RL circuit τ = L/R.
Capacitors in parallel add: C = C₁ + C₂. In series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. Inductors behave like resistors.

lessons.title: Magnetic fields · Force on a wire

cards.t: Magnets and moving charges make magnetic fields, measured in tesla (T). Field lines run from north to south outside the magnet.
A wire of length L carrying current I in a field B feels force F = BIL when the wire is at right angles to the field.

lab.hook: A wire with current in a magnetic field feels a push.

cards.t: A charge q moving at speed v across field B feels F = qvB. The force is sideways, so the charge goes in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB).
A changing magnetic flux induces a voltage: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt (Faraday's law). Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change.
Two coils on one iron core: V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁. A step-up transformer raises voltage and lowers current.

lab.hook: A transformer changes voltage by the turns ratio.

lessons.title: Magnetic force on a charge · Circular paths

cards.t: A charge moving across a magnetic field feels a force F = qvB sin θ, at right angles to both v and B (right-hand rule). The force does no work, so speed stays constant.
A charge moving at right angles to B goes in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB), with period T = 2πm/(qB).
A current-carrying wire in a field feels F = BIL sin θ.

lessons.title: Field of a current · Faraday's law

cards.t: A long straight wire makes B = μ₀I/(2πr), with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. A solenoid has B = μ₀nI inside, where n is turns per metre.
A changing magnetic flux induces an emf: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt. Flux Φ = BA cos θ.
The induced current opposes the change that caused it. A rod of length L moving at v across a field B has emf ε = BLv.
Alternating current swings back and forth like a sine wave. Wall power is 60 Hz in the US: 60 full cycles each second.

lab.hook: AC voltage swings back and forth.

cards.t: The RMS value gives the same heating as DC. For a sine wave V_rms = V_peak/√2 ≈ 0.707 V_peak. US outlets are 120 V rms.

lab.hook: RMS is the steady voltage that heats like the AC.
lab.note: {=v/1.414|1} V rms. The wall outlet: 170 V peak ≈ 120 V rms.

cards.t: A capacitor resists AC by X_C = 1/(2πfC); an inductor by X_L = 2πfL. Units: ohms. Capacitors pass high frequencies, inductors pass low ones.
Resistance and reactance combine at right angles: |Z| = √(R² + X²) for a series RL or RC circuit. Ohm's law becomes V = IZ.
Only the resistive part uses real power: P = V·I·cos φ, where cos φ = R/|Z| is the power factor.
A filter treats frequencies differently. A low-pass filter keeps low frequencies, a high-pass keeps high ones, and a band-pass keeps a range.
An RC filter drops to 70.7% (−3 dB) of the input at the cutoff frequency f_c = 1/(2πRC).

lab.hook: A low-pass filter lets low frequencies through.

cards.t: Decibels compare sizes on a log scale: dB = 20 log₁₀(V_out/V_in) for voltage. Every factor of 10 is 20 dB; halving is about −6 dB.
A series LC circuit has the lowest impedance at f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)), where X_L = X_C. Radios tune by changing this frequency.
Q = f₀/bandwidth tells how sharp the resonance is. A series RLC has Q = X_L/R at resonance.
A diode lets current go one way. Silicon needs about 0.7 V forward; an LED needs roughly 2 V. Always add a series resistor.
The resistor drops the leftover voltage: R = (V_supply − V_LED)/I.
A diode on an AC source blocks the negative half (half-wave). A bridge of four diodes flips the negative half (full-wave). A capacitor then smooths it.
A small base current controls a big collector current: I_C = β·I_B. It works as a switch or an amplifier.
An op-amp with negative feedback has two golden rules: no current into the inputs and equal input voltages. Inverting gain = −R_f/R_in; non-inverting gain = 1 + R_f/R_in.
Computers use only 0 and 1. Each place is a power of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... so 1011₂ = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.

lab.hook: Flip the switches to count in binary.
lab.say: Each switch is worth double the one on its right.
lab.take: Binary uses only 0 and 1. Each place is a power of 2.

cards.t: Hex uses 16 digits (0–9, A–F). One hex digit equals four bits: A = 1010, F = 1111.
AND is 1 only if both inputs are 1. OR is 1 if either is 1. NOT flips the bit. NAND and NOR are the opposites of AND and OR.

lab.hook: Flip A and B. When is the lamp on?
lab.take: AND: both must be 1. OR: either one.

lessons.title: Truth tables · Converting analog to digital

cards.t: A truth table lists the output for every input combination. n inputs give 2ⁿ rows.

lab.hook: Try OR. Then compare with AND.

cards.t: An n-bit converter splits its range into 2ⁿ levels. Step size = full-scale voltage ÷ 2ⁿ.

lessons.title: Electric power · Why power lines use high voltage

cards.t: Power is P = VI = I²R = V²/R, in watts. A kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the energy of 1 kW used for 1 hour, or 3.6 million joules.

cards.h: Why power lines use high voltage
cards.t: Wire loss is I²R. Raising the voltage by 10× cuts the current for the same power by 10× and the loss by 100×.

lab.hook: Same power at higher voltage means less current and far less loss.
lab.note: Loss falls as 1/V². At {v} kV the loss is {=1/v^2|4} of the loss at 1 kV.

cards.t: Efficiency = useful output power ÷ input power. The difference leaves as heat.
Power plants use three sine waves 120° apart. Total power is √3·V_line·I_line·cos φ.
Light comes in packets. A photon has energy E = hf = hc/λ. A handy form: E (eV) = 1240 / λ (nm).
A photon frees an electron only if its energy exceeds the metal's work function φ. The fastest electrons leave with KE_max = hf − φ. Brighter light means more electrons, not faster ones.
Particles have a wavelength λ = h/p. Electrons diffract, which is why electron microscopes see fine detail.
Hydrogen energy levels are E_n = −13.6 eV / n². A photon is emitted or absorbed when the electron jumps between levels.
Unstable nuclei decay at random, but a large sample halves every half-life: N = N₀ (½)^(t/T½).
Mass is a form of energy: E = mc². In nuclear reactions the lost mass shows up as energy: 1 u of mass equals 931.5 MeV.
